etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a contraction of いらせらる (iraseraru), itself an honorific conjugation of 入ら (ira, the 未然形 (mizenkei, “imperfective”) of verb iru, “to come in, to go in; to arrive; to be in a place”) + せ (se, the 未然形 (mizenkei, “imperfective”) of honorific auxiliary verb su) + らる (raru, the older form of passivizing auxiliary verb rareru, here serving as another honorific).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of particle で (de, “at, in, on”, locative particle) and は (wa, topic particle; no English equivalent). In this case, the は (wa) is used in its contrastive function, emphasizing that the statement is about the portion preceding the で (de) in contrast to other possibilities.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Of で (de, conjunctive adverb) and は (wa, topic particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of ではないか (de wa nai ka, “isn't it; might it be”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First cited to 1604 in the Portuguese work Arte da Lingoa de Iapam.
The initial ど (do) may be cognate with the interrogative ど (do) seen in どれ (dore), どこ (doko), どち (dochi).
Alternatively, possibly from older form だう (dau), much like the shift from かう (kau) → こう (kō, “like this, this way”), or さう (sau) → そう (sō, “like that, that way”). This shift is apparently suggested in the Arte da Lingoa de Iapam entry of Dǒxô, presumably どうしよう (dō shiyō). However, the expected entries dǒ or dǒxô are missing from the 1603 Nippo Jisho.
The kanji spelling is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), using the corresponding Chinese term for the spelling and the underlying Japanese root word for the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nani semu ni/ → */nanzenni/ → /nazenni/ → /nazeni/ → /naze/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
The ge element is likely related to 毛 (ke, “hair, fur”), but further etymology is uncertain. Possibilities include:
* Shift from hohoge (頬 (hoho, “cheek”) + 毛 (ke)) or from hirege (鰭 (hire, “fin”) + 毛 (ke)). Both theories are unlikely unless the term originally referred only to cheek hair.
* Shift from hirakuke (開く (hiraku, “to open”) + 毛 (ke)), literally, “hair of the opening”. This would include other hair around the mouth, although “opening” being used to mean the mouth is unlikely.
* Shift from hege (辺 (he) + 毛 (ke)) or herige (縁 (heri, “edge”) + 毛 (ke)), literally, “edge hair”. Compare 唇 (kuchiberi) being from 口 (kuchi, “mouth”) + 縁 (heri), literally, “mouth edge”.
* The hi element being cognate with Korean 입 (ip, “mouth”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from American English elevator.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Transliteration of English humour or humor.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 一(いち) (ichi, “one”) + 杯(はい) (hai, “cupful”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kautuː/ → /kɔːt͡suː/ → /koːt͡suː/
From Middle Chinese compound 交通 (kaew thuwng, literally “cross through”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 別(わか)れる (wakareru, “to separate, to part ways, to bid farewell, to break up”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 句 (kjuᴴ, “phrase”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pəyu. Cognate with Kunigami 吠いるん (ぶいるん, buirun), Miyako 吠いㇲ゙ (ぶいㇲ゙, buiz).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 幕 (MC mak).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 待(ま)ち合(あ)い (machiai, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 待(ま)ち合(あ)う (machiau)) + 室(しつ) (-shitsu, “room”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 心(しん) (shin, “heart”) + 臓(ぞう) (zō, “internal organ”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of the verbs 感ずる (kanzuru) and 感じる (kanjiru, “to feel”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 拡(かく) (kaku, “expand”) + 張(ちょう) (chō, “stretch”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 洋品(ようひん) (yōhin) + 店(てん) (-ten)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 深(ふか) (fuka, root of 深(ふか)い (fukai, “deep, profound”)) + まる (-maru, “to become (an adjective), -en”), developed from Classical Japanese 深(ふか)む (fukamu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 火山 (xwa^X srean, literally “flaming mountain”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 無 (MC mju). The 呉音 (goon), so likely an earlier borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 無 (bu). The 漢音 (kan'on), so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 矛盾 (MC mjuw zywinX), literally 矛 (“lance, spear”) + 盾 (“shield”). See the Chinese etymology section for the full derivation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 研究 (ngen *kiuᴴ?). Compare modern Hakka ngiên-kiu, Eastern Min ngiĕng-géu, Min Nan gián-kiù.
The original on'yomi for the first character 研 was gen, more closely matching the Chinese origins. For reasons unknown, the reading shifted from gen to a kan'yō yomi of ken.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nau/ → /nɔː/ → /noː/
From Middle Chinese 腦 (MC nawX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨naduki₁⟩ → */nadukʲi/ → /nad͡zuki/ → /nazuki/
From Old Japanese.
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical verb 漬(なず)く (nazuku, “to be immersed in water (or other liquid)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Proto-Japonic *kusori. Appears to be the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or noun form”) of unattested verb kusuru “to have a mystical effect”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Cognate with the kusu root of adjective 奇し (kusushi, “mystical”), from the way that drugs and medicines would have mystical effects. It is not clear whether this is a contraction or the original form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 藥 (MC yak). Compare modern Cantonese 藥／药 (joek6).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 踏(ふ)み (fumi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 踏(ふ)む (fumu, “step on, tread on, stamp”).) + 切(き)り (kiri, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 切(き)る (kiru, “perform an action as if by cutting”).).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Sinitic 農家 /农家 (nóngjiā).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Sinitic 通譯 /通译 (tōngyì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 電(でん) (den, “electric”) + 力(りょく) (-ryoku, “power”).
